steps.text: Gather all ingredients. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Rinse and wash turkey. Discard the giblets, or add to pan if they are anyone's favorites.

Place turkey in a Dutch oven or roasting pan. Separate the skin over the breast to make little pockets. Put 3 tablespoons of the butter on both sides between the skin and breast meat. This makes for very juicy breast meat.
In a medium bowl, combine the water with the bouillon. Sprinkle in the parsley and minced onion. Pour over the top of the turkey. Sprinkle seasoning salt over the turkey.
Cover with foil, and bake in the preheated oven 3 1/2 to 4 hours, until the internal temperature of the turkey reaches 180 degrees F (80 degrees C).
For the last 45 minutes or so, remove the foil so the turkey will brown nicely.

raw_recipe.headline: Homestyle Turkey, the Michigander Way
raw_recipe.description: Here's a simple recipe for preparing the holiday bird. It will be tasty and perfectly browned every time!

review.reviewBody: This was the best turkey I have ever made or eaten. I could not believe how moist and tender the breast was! My thanksgiving was made perfect with this delicious bird. Everyone asked how I did it, even my elderly aunt, who is the best cook ever, raved about it. I used about a stick and a half of butter under the skin. I buttered that bird good. I also rubbed the outside of the bird with butter before pouring the boullion mixture and before the seasoned salt. It was such a beautiful golden brown. I was so busy that day that I only got it basted a couple of times during cooking, but it couldn't have been any better or jucier. This was a 21 pound bird, and I cooked it for 1 hour at 375 degrees then reduced to 350 degrees for 5 more hours to reach 180 degrees. Perfect!!! Thanks a million Robin!!

This is my favorite way to make turkey. I do it in a bag, which I believe makes it more moist. As written (with the bag), I would strongly recommend this. I recently changed this up just a tad. The night before cooking, I rubbed the turkey with the seasoning salt, parsley and about 1 Tbsp. of dried rosemary. Then I added the butter and slid some sliced lemons in between the skin and the meat. That sat all night. Just before popping it in the oven, I dumped the chicken broth around the outside. I totally forgot the onions. The result was an amazing flavored, moist turkey. I will do it this way again.

Absolutely amazing! I did a brine of vegetable and chicken stock and let it sit for 24+hrs. I also added chopped onions, carrots, celery to the bottom of the pan, to cook along with the Turkey. I then filled the bottom with chicken broth so I could baste the Turkey throughout cooking time. I used cheese cloth to stuff the Turkey with the dressing, which was my sausage recipe I always do. We ended up by accident not covering the Turkey for the first 30-45 mins which actually sealed the Turkey nicely to keep the moisture in. We then covered with foil and I basted the Turkey about 2-3x more throughout the cooking time. Let’s just say, it came out heavenly! And I used the drippings and veggies at the bottom for the soup I made the next day, after sticking the Turkey in a “bath” to get the rest of the meat off. I combined the turkey stock, veggies and left over dressing. I let it sit in the fridge overnight so the fat would settled at the top, I scraped that up and it was enjoyed by all and lots left over to freeze for yummy turkey soup in the winter!

I had a 21 pounder due to the amount of guests coming to the Thanksgiving feast, so I was pretty worried about how the end result would be for a bigger turkey.... maybe too dry or burnt. However, it totally came out perfect. Everyone raved about how tasty and juicy it was. 

Just a few side notes I wanted to mention. For the size of the turkey, I used 8 tablespoons of butter (so 4 on each side). I would use the same amount of bouillon, water and herbs as original recipe states. You really don't need to double up, because you're just pouring the broth over the turkey to coat. Also, I recommend using a meat oven thermometer, because sometimes you just never know how long the turkey will take to roast until it gets to 180 degrees. The first hour I roasted at 375 and then I lowered it to 350 degrees. Because our oven was actually smaller, the total roast time was 3.0 hrs flat. I couldn't believe it. But, our temperature gauge didn't lie. Enjoy!!!

Most of the method used in this recipe is good but the quantities and a couple things make no sense. Luckily I've done my share of cooking and changed a few things. I've tried the butter under the skin a couple times before, and I've tried injecting and I've tried cooking uncovered and basting. Injecting can make for good turkey, but it tends to make a lot of spots with lots of flavor and lots of spots with little flavor and also makes a lot of holes for juices to escape. I think the best method is seasoned butter under the skin and outside the skin and cooking covered until the last 45 mins then browning. This results in a flavorful and moist turkey with almost no effort while cooking.

I cooked a 20lb turkey. First, 4 cups of water is way too much, even for a 20lb turkey. I added about 1.5 cups of bone broth over the turkey and ended up with the large roasting pan almost overflowing with juice and fat. Second, putting your herbs into the water/broth and pouring it over the turkey does nothing except add liquid to the bottom of the pan. Third, 4 hours is too long for a 12lb turkey.

I defrosted my 20lb turkey for almost 6 days. I mixed a cube of butter with sage, thyme, salt, and minced garlic and spread it around under the skin of the breast and legs and all around the outside of the turkey. Who says you have to wait until November to cook a turkey? We wanted cold turkey sandwiches in this triple digit summer here in the desert so I decide to do this one on the BBQ in order to keep from heating up the house. They may do it in Michigan but here in California we don't cook our birds to 180 degrees. Cooking times are for guesstimates. The only real way to know when your bird is done is to use a remote probe thermometer. I pulled the bird when it reached 157 degrees and let it push the the temp to 167 for a tender juicy bird with crispy skin. I also mixed in some extra parsley and minced onion with the butter and placed under the skin of the breast. Don't overcook your turkey unless you like turkey jerky. Depending on the size of your turkey the temp can raise as much as 10 degrees after removing it from the heat source.

I am very pleased with how this turned out. We didn’t have dried minced onion, so I sprinkled some chalots and garlic on top. I stuffed it with stuffing, which may have worked to keep moisture in, too. My Dutch oven is a bit small so I didn’t use all of the chicken boullion. I also didn’t have seasoning salt so I just used some paprika, salt and pepper. It turned out very moist and juicy. I didn’t baste once. It was a 12 lb bird and took about 4 hours.

Perfect turkey!! The Greatest secret is butter under the breast skin to keep it moist. I’ve tried over a dozen recipes and this Is the best. I end up putting the bird on a rotisserie in the BBQ in order to free up oven space. I use indirect heat and put a disposable foil pan under the turkey to prevent flare ups and catch drippings for gravy as desired. It makes for an evenly browned turkey with super easy cleanup.
Rotisserie Cook time is 10-15 min per lb, put scrap veggies and liquid in the drip pan to help increase moisture and control temperature. Refill the liquid while the turkey cooks.

I've always added liquid to the pan when roasting a turkey along with bouillon cubes and butter. Never understood why so many professionals tell you not to add any liquid. Rated four stars because there's no mention of this: For juiciness and tenderness, I've learned to always brine that bird first. And you don't need to get all fancy with the brine recipe to get a tender and juicy result, just flip it over halfway through the brining process. To roast, thoroughly rinse the turkey inside and out; pat it dry. Stuff the turkey if desired. Place it in the pan and rub it down with olive oil. Sprinkle with your herb(s) of choice. Add water or chicken broth/stock to about 1/4", 2-3 chicken bouillon cubes, several small blobs of butter, and about 1/2 cup of chopped celery. Tent the breast and drumsticks with aluminum foil and pop it into the oven. After about 1-1/2 hours, start basting periodically; add a little water to the pan as needed. When you come down to the final 30-45 minutes, remove the tent to allow the breast and legs to brown. I'm looking (fondly) at a big ol' tom turkey in the field behind my house right now . . . LOL!
Poultry and meat should never ever be washed. Highly dangerous. Additionally never discard any giblets as they make gorgeous gravy.

Made a few adjustments- loved it! My notes/changes below:

-12 lb turkey
-340 oven
- 3/4 stick butter rubbed inside skin with a few chunks left in
-Stuffed with packet of stuffing, mixed with celery
-placed 3/4 onion in the middle
-Seasones turkey with salt pepper, montreal chicken
- Covered turkey with 4 cups beef broth with parsley, basil, and paprika with remains pooling in roastin pan
-cut up potatoes and put in broth of roastin pan
-cooked at 340, basting every 30 minutes for 3:15
-removed foil tent at 45 minutes to removal. Total cook time 4 hrs
I have used this recipe every Thanksgiving for the past 10 years. It's definitely a family favorite! Always comes out so juicy. Thank you for sharing this recipe.

I have used this recipe many, many times over the past few decades. It’s always perfect. The only thing I alter is… after removing the turkey from the oven I sprinkle fresh parsley. I do add dry parsley to the broth when I place everything in the oven but the presentation with fresh parsley is nice. A few sprigs at the base of the turkey works well.
I’ve made this recipe many times and every time it has produced a tender, moist, delicious turkey. So easy to follow. I highly recommend!

First time I ever made a turkey for the family the pressure was ON! Since then I’ve slightly modified my ingredients because the second or third year I was missing items I’d forgotten. But EVERY time I do this it’s fall apart tender. The first year my mom and I were transferring it from the foil roasting pan to a cutting table and a wing literally fell off. We looked at each other and said “Well, that’s a good sign!” This is now my 5th straight Thanksgiving that I’m expected to make the turkey. Here’s my modifications/adjustments: based on size of turkey I’ll double this. And I still do the butter under the skin and use seasoning salt to my hearts desire. 4 cups chicken broth 2 tblsp chicken seasoning 2 tblsp dried parsley 2 tblsp dried onion 2 tblsp garlic powder 2 tblsp thyme
Don't put the parsley on top of the turkey, all you get is dry crunchy bits. Double everything else and enjoy
